content.thinking:
I'm planning the gnome's proportions and skeleton layout, aiming for about 1.1 meters tall with a chunky torso, big head, and short legs, and I'm working out joint coordinates starting from the hips upward.

Continuing to figure out chains...

Now I'm defining the leg joints symmetrically for both sides—hip, knee, ankle—as a chain parented to hips with the tip aimed downward, then adding toe joints for the feet.

For the boots, I'm building separate geometric parts: a cylinder for the shaft and a scaled sphere for the toe, attached to the ankle bone.

Still adding boot pieces...

Then I'm checking that the sole box and toe sphere sit flush with the floor at y=0 so the character doesn't float or clip.

For the pants, I'm sweeping along the leg chain with tapering radii from hip to ankle in an olive-green color, keeping the caps rounded. For the torso, I'm sweeping a circular cross-section along the spine chain with varying radii to give it a chunky belly shape.

Now I'm thinking through the vest and shirt coloring — a brown mottled vest over a cream shirt visible at the chest V, with the torso radius keys tuned so hips, chest, and waist taper naturally into the flared tunic skirt.

For the skirt tails I'll shape a cone frustum cylinder geometry sitting at the hip line to form the front flap, painted brown with mottling to match the tunic, then add a belt as a slightly wider closed cylinder sitting just above the torso's natural radius at the waist.

Now I'm sizing the brass belt buckle as a small box with a darker inset, positioning the tunic skirt cylinder so its top sits near the waist and flares wider at the bottom to reveal short pants and boots below, then working out the shoulder, elbow, and wrist joint positions for the arms.

For the pose, I'm keeping both arms neutral and slightly outstretched rather than matching the reference's raised arm, naming the arm chain bones per side and parenting them to the chest with cream sleeve cylinders tapering toward the wrist. For hands, I'm simplifying to a fist sphere at the wrist plus a thumb, skipping individual finger joints since full digit articulation would add too many parts.

I'm adding a single simple finger joint chain per hand for basic rigging, with brown glove coloring and a brass-studded cuff cylinder at the wrist. The hand orientation aligns with the wrist bone's end tangent using vector math to compute direction and offset. For the head, I'm placing a large spherical head joint at the neck with a bulbous nose feature.

Now I'm sketching out the ear geometry, trying a spike/cone shape first, then switching to an extruded outline approach with pointed, flattened ear profiles positioned outward from the head.

For the beard, I'm planning a layered loft structure, stacking stations from chin down through the jaw with decreasing width and height to create a tapered white-grey beard shape.

Now I'm adding beard texture with mottled shading and spike locks along the lower edge, plus a swept mustache made of curled strands, bushy eyebrow sweeps, and small spherical eyes with white sclera and dark pupils positioned on the head's surface using offset geometry from the head center.

Now I'm planning the facial features—pink cheek spheres, a protruding peach nose on the head surface, and subtle blush decals. I'm also designing brass octagonal goggles for the forehead band using oriented cylinders, with smaller teal glass lenses for a glowing effect.

For the strap and hat, I'm calculating circle radii using the head sphere geometry so the goggle band sits correctly at head height, then shaping a tilted gnome-style hat as a swept cone curving back and up from a wide base near the head's top, keeping the total height within the figure's budget.

Checking that the hat radius clears the eyes and head properly, I realize using a flat starting disc at a slightly higher y avoids overlapping the face, since the circular cross-section there only needs to cover the top of the head.

For hair, I'll add a ring of white spike cones tucked under the hat brim, rigged to the head, placed around a circle at the base height and angled outward and slightly forward to look like tufts peeking out.

Now I'm working out the goggle strap band: a closed ring wrapping the hat just above its base, tapering with the hat's radius, with a brass buckle on front and two cylindrical goggle lenses mounted onto the band just above center.

Next I'm sketching the backpack, a chunky box parented to the chest bone with a darker lid piece, positioned so its front edge overlaps the torso's back curvature. I'm considering adding a horizontal barrel-shaped detail to the pack for visual texture.

Adding brass corner caps and shoulder straps...

I should add shoulder caps where the sleeves meet, plus a chest strap with a small brass ring. For the pack gadgets, I'm thinking of a big cogwheel on the top-left, built by generating a toothed polygon outline programmatically and extruding it into a thin gear shape with a dark axle cap, oriented to face outward from the pack's back.

Now I'm placing items on the back face of the pack: a brass boiler-style sphere with a chimney on top, positioned above the trunk, figuring out coordinates so it sits correctly relative to the waist belt and pack bottom.

Adding chimney cap and rim rings, double-checking the hat tip and chimney don't collide since they're both positioned toward the back. Now I'm setting up a copper coil spring using a helical sweep path near the boiler.

Still placing the clock gadget...

Now I'm adding a hanging lantern on the left with a glowing orange glass body, brass cap and ring handle, plus a glowing teal potion flask with a corked neck and brass cage on the right side, and starting a horizontal scroll prop near the back.

I'm reconsidering placement to avoid overlap, deciding to put the clock and lantern on the left side, the gear, gauge, and small pouch on the back face, and the flask with a wrench bundle on the right side.

Now I'm positioning the boiler, chimney, coil, and antenna with a dish on top, and a horizontal scroll tied under the pack at the bottom back. For the front, I'm adding a leather tool pouch on the hip with a wrench and screwdriver peeking out, including a brass stud and strap, and sketching a simple wrench outline shape with a handle and open jaw head.

I'll fix the axis orientation so x and y are orthogonal, then set thickness for the wrench. For the other tools, I'm planning a cylindrical screwdriver with a thick wooden handle, and a hammer made from a rod handle plus a box-shaped head, hanging from a loop on the left hip.

Now I want to add a bandolier strap across the chest with small vials attached, draping a diagonal path from the right shoulder to the left hip against the torso surface so it conforms naturally, then placing a sweep box section and small vials spaced along that path.

I'm also thinking about a shirt collar (likely hidden beneath the beard), and keeping the torso as a painted vest with cream arms, maybe adding a small stitched pocket detail on the chest. For rigging, I'm planning root hips, a spine chain, neck/head joint, and a separate jaw joint so the mouth and beard can animate with upper and lower jaw parts.

Working out joint placement for the jaw under the head, using local offsets relative to the head joint rather than world coordinates, since the head itself sits atop an upward-curving neck chain and I need to be careful about which axis counts as "up" versus "forward" for aiming the joints correctly.

Simplifying the approach: I'll build the neck as a two-point chain (one span, named "neck") attached to the chest joint from the spine chain, then add the head as a separate joint parented to the neck tip, with its direction pointing forward-ish rather than purely vertical.

For the spine chain itself, I'm plotting three points rising from y=.44 to y=.76 for two spans plus a tip, noting the hip joint shares the same base position as spine1. I'll let the torso sweep's rounded caps handle shoulder and head clearance, checking that the cap radius keeps the top around y=.89 so the head (centered near y=.96 with radius .115, bottom at .845) sits just above without excessive overlap.

I'll trim the end radius down to around .11 so the cap top lands closer to .87, keeping things tidy under the beard. For the tunic I'm mottling a dark tunic color variant onto the torso sweep for texture. For the face, I'm making the jaw a small hidden flesh-colored box under the beard, with the lower beard geometry rigged to loft along the jaw bone so it moves naturally with speech, while the moustache and nose stay fixed to the head. I'm defining the jaw joint as a child of the head with its position and aim set near the chin, then shaping the jaw part as a small flattened sphere.

Now I'm working out how parts attach to the right bones — since the jaw is a child of head, I need to explicitly assign a "head" bone to all head parts rather than relying on automatic nearest-joint detection, so I'm writing a small helper function to simplify that binding per body part. I'm also laying out the full joint hierarchy: hips as root, a spine chain, neck, head, jaw, arm chains ending in wrist joints with finger and thumb joints, leg chains ending in ankle and toe joints, plus a backpack joint with a hinge-type lid joint positioned at the back of the pack. I'm also considering making the hat a small joint chain itself so it can sweep like a tail, though I need to check which role types are valid for that.

I'm settling on treating the hat tip as a 3-span chain (using "tail" as its role even though it's a loose fit) parented to the head, built from a catmull curve with flat-to-point end caps, and now I'm thinking about how to decorate the hat with patches and a stitched decal, positioning them against the swept surface with an appropriate normal direction.

Now I'm tallying up the full color palette to make sure I stay under the 64-colour limit—skin tones, beard whites, hat reds, leather browns, tunic and pants shades, and various metal tones for brass, copper, and steel parts.

Then I'm planning the surface detailing: wood grain on the pack, stitching lines, and panel strips, before setting up the imports needed for the build script, making sure only the helper functions I'll actually use (like the builder, catmull curves, and spiral paths) are included.

Setting up the gnome's skeleton...

I'm trying to figure out whether passing a Chain directly as the parent or bone works, since JointRef might accept a Chain in addition to a Joint or its name, but I'm not fully certain of the type definition.

Adding neck and head joints...

Still defining leg chains and joints...

Still writing boot geometry...

Setting the torus rotation to align its axis with Y, skipping laces, adding two rivets. For the arms I'm defining the joint chain shoulder-elbow-wrist with a tapered sleeve radius profile in mottled cream tones, parented to the chest, and considering a leather epaulette for the shoulder pad.

Now I'm computing the arm direction vector from elbow to wrist to position a cuff cylinder near the wrist, using a lerp along that vector and a helper point function for the coordinates.

For the hand itself, I'll use a slightly squashed sphere for the palm and fist shape, then add four small finger boxes spaced across the width plus a thumb, positioning them along the forearm direction with a perpendicular side offset so the fingers curl naturally toward the front.

For the belt and torso accessories, I'm working through the sweep geometry's vertex radius versus circumscribed radius, since the detail-scaled side count was coming out too low (6 sides at detail .8). I'll set torso sides explicitly to 10 and size the belt radius to account for the vertex-to-face radius ratio at that polygon count.

Now I'm placing the buckle: a brass box at the belt front with an inset darker box for depth, figuring out which radial vertex faces forward based on the cylinder's angular start point. Then I'm sizing the tunic skirt as a tapered cylinder wider than the torso, spanning from waist down to mid-thigh.

Working out two front tabard panels tilted to match the skirt's outward slope — calculating the slope angle from the skirt's radius difference and rotating the panels around the x-axis to match, with brown base color and a yellow zigzag trim.

Now I'm sketching chest pockets, then moving to torso decor — draping a bandolier along a swept spine path using a catmull curve through five points, with a box cross-section for the strap.

Mapping out the bandolier's path points from shoulder to hip, then placing small glass-colored vial cylinders along it using frame data from each path point.

Still adding collar geometry and skipping chest details. For the beard, I'm lofting a jaw-mounted shape with mottled paint and a subtle grain texture along the vertical axis to give it a streaky, hair-like look.

For extra detail, I'm adding spike elements beneath the beard to simulate individual locks, anchoring them to the jaw bone so they move naturally with the head. The beard's front projection stays within the torso's silhouette, and since the jaw is already a child bone of the head, everything should follow correctly.

Still positioning facial features...

Adding tiny pupil highlights, then sweeping bushy white eyebrow curves above the eyes and checking they tuck under the hat brim by raising the hat's starting height to 1.05 so the brows don't poke through.

Now I'm shaping the floppy hat with a drooping chain of points curving down and back for a gnome-style tip, tapering the radius through several keyframes so it narrows to a point, bringing the total hat height to about 1.27, giving the gnome a total height near 1.1m with the hat.

For the brim I'm adding a torus ring at the base of the hat, then working out the goggle band position by interpolating along the hat's curve to find the right y-height, z-offset, and radius, placing eight points evenly around that circle for the band geometry.

For the goggles themselves I'm placing two lens assemblies symmetrically on either side of center, using brass-colored outer cylinders and glass-colored inner cylinders sized so the pair sits close without overlapping.

Checking the depth placement, I want the goggle's back face to roughly meet the hat brim's front curve, so I'm nudging the center z value slightly to around .155 to avoid a floating gap.

Then for hair, I'm sweeping a ring of spikes around the head between about -110° and 110°, computing each base point on a small radius circle and projecting the tip outward and downward to give that spiky punk look.

Now I'm working out the ears -- an extruded outline shape positioned and rotated so it tilts up and out from the head, colored skin tone, plus a smaller inner extrusion in pink for the ear's inner detail.

Next I'm adding pink cheek spheres positioned relative to the head center, tinting the nose slightly redder, and applying a mottled skin texture for subtle color variation on the face. For the head itself I'm using a low-poly flat-shaded sphere, scaled slightly to widen it. Now I'm starting on the backpack, beginning with its attachment joint.

Setting up the pack's lid hinge and gear joints with aim directions, then building the trunk as a painted wood-grain box with brass corner caps, considering whether to merge the cap geometries or keep them as individual pieces for simplicity.

Now I'm adding the metal straps wrapping the trunk as brass plate bands with rivet details spaced along the back face.

For the lid itself, I'm positioning it hinged at the back with proper geometry origin offset, then adding a small arched torus handle on top using a half-circle arc shape.

Now I'm working on the pack's back-face gadgets, starting with a brass gear decoration: an extruded gear outline with teeth, a darker hub cylinder, and spoke boxes radiating outward, all positioned on the back panel.

Still writing the gear-tooth polygon geometry...

Then I'm planning a pressure gauge detail: a small brass cylinder on the back with a circular face textured with a gauge dial, oriented to face backward with a pink-red danger zone painted into the texture.

For the pipework, I'm sketching a copper tube running from the gauge up to the boiler using a curved path of waypoints, with a small radius and hexagonal cross-section to give it that riveted steampunk look.

Now I'm building the boiler itself: a brass sphere scaled slightly for a barrel shape, wrapped with a torus band, topped with a cylindrical chimney, a conical cap, and a rim ring, all positioned to line up with the trunk and lid geometry below.

I want to add a few small puff spheres above the chimney for smoke, but they'd collide with the hat tip, so I'm shifting the whole boiler/chimney assembly a bit to the side to make room, then placing two small puffs that clear the hat by a safe margin. Now moving on to adding a small pressure valve detail on the boiler.

Writing coil spiral code...

I'm adjusting the coil so its base sits right at the lid top, letting it emerge through the lid rather than floating above it, with a small brass cylinder anchoring its base. Then I'm considering adding a telescoping spyglass element on the back/side, positioned near the flask with cylinders stepping outward at a slight tilt.

I'm placing the spyglass as three stacked tapered rod segments running up the trunk's right-back corner, using straps to tie them down, and checking clearances against the nearby gear so the parts don't overlap.

Now I'm placing the clock on the left side—a brass cylinder body with a face plane and bezel torus, plus a small top button, then setting up a lantern bracket rod extending out from the trunk.

Working out the lantern's hexagonal glass body with amber glow, brass base and cap, ring, and six thin corner posts, while checking it doesn't collide with the clock hanging above it.

Now I'm adding a teal glowing flask on the right side with a neck, cork, a brass cage band, a strap mount, and a connecting rod to the trunk, then starting on a scroll cylinder tucked under the pack.

Checking the scroll's placement against the pack bottom so it clears the floor, then adding rolled end caps and a red ribbon tie wrapped around it. Now I'm sketching a small leather pouch for the back, positioning it near the gear and gauge on the left side.

Thinking about adding a tiny spinning propeller gadget on top of the pack, near the hat tip—working out the rod position and blade geometry using horizontal extrusions.

Adding the mast cylinder beneath the blades and checking the hat clears them vertically, then I'm placing belt tools -- a hammer on the left hip and a pouch with a wrench and screwdriver up front.

I'm adding chest decals too: small brass button spheres arranged in rows on the vest, using surface ray-casts against the torso to position them accurately, plus thinking about a pocket patch and bandolier drape.

Checking the bandolier path from shoulder to hip against the beard's position — since the beard sits centered and the bandolier runs diagonally, they shouldn't conflict much. I'm also considering adding a wrench or small tool to a hand, but may skip that for simplicity. Now moving to designing SVG textures for a clock face, gauge, and hat patch, starting with a circular clock face design.

Writing SVG code...

Adding gear-like ring detail...

I'll keep the leather mottle texture and paint atlas at the current resolution, and make sure the total part count stays reasonably bounded, roughly under 500.

For the lower body, I'm placing the soles exactly at floor level, adding a torus-shaped hem trim in a brass/gold tone around the skirt bottom, and positioning the boots inward within the skirt's radius so everything nests properly. Now I'm writing a helper function for generating box geometries.

Defining placement helper...

Still writing arm geometry...

Still rigging the hand bones...

Finishing the thumb placement, I move to the shoulder pad sphere positioning and bone naming, then work through the pack strap paths with their catmull curve control points mirrored across sides.

I decide against draping these straps onto the torso surface since points near the shoulder would snap awkwardly to the torso's top cap, pulling the strap out of shape—better to keep them as plain paths. Now I'm defining the strap sweep as a flat box cross-section with leather coloring, running from the pack top down past the underarms to the pack bottom.

For the chest strap, I notice a straight rod between the two straps would pierce through the torso geometry at that height, so I switch to draping it as a curved polyline that arcs in front of the chest instead of cutting a straight chord through the body.

Actually since the beard covers this area anyway, I decide to skip the chest strap entirely and just keep the bandolier -- the pack's bottom strap setup should be sufficient. I'm now defining the torso as a sweep along the spine with a tapering radius profile, then building a surface over it so I can raycast button positions, keeping them off-center at roughly ±.05 so they don't land hidden under the beard.

Since the beard covers most of the center chest down to about y=.58, I decide to abandon the button idea altogether and instead focus detail on belt pouches and hip loops on either side, placing a front-right pouch box near the skirt's lower radius and working out its circumradius position.

I'm calculating the yaw rotation needed so the pouch faces outward along the correct radial direction, then positioning a wrench sticking out of it.

I'm designing a generic pouch placement function that positions items at an angle around the belt, with the right side carrying a wrench and screwdriver, and the left side given a simpler pouch. For the yaw rotation, I'm working out how angle θ maps to position coordinates using sine and cosine so the pouch orientation faces outward correctly.

Now I'm detailing the pouch's parts: a brown body box, a lighter flap on top, a center strap, and a small brass stud, all placed using a helper that converts local coordinates into world position and rotation based on the belt radius and angle. I'm also starting to hang a hammer at the left hip with a loop ring and a handle rod extending down from a fixed point.

Working out hammer head placement...

Now I'm deciding to simplify by making a generic pouch function with a boolean for tools, giving the left pouch two screwdrivers using rod-based geometry for shaft and handle, positioned with relative offsets and slight tilt.

The skirt should attach to the hips bone for a rigid sweep, with the pack as a child joint of the chest and a small hem trim on the tunic. Now I'm defining the full color palette for skin, beard, hair, and hat tones before writing the complete code.

Still defining colors...

Writing gear outline function...

Now I'm setting up the extrude options for the gear bone with thickness and bevel, then adding a hat decal positioned near the hat sweep surface at a specific offset and direction, before finalizing and returning the build root.

I'm adding a small brass bell sphere at the tip of the hat chain, computed from the path's final point, then cleaning up unused imports and variables. I'm defining the hat chain bones and building its catmull-rom path through the knot points, then setting up the hat sweep profile with tapering radii, paint color, octagonal sides, and flat-to-point end caps.

Checking that the flat start cap faces downward correctly, verifying the hat's mottled paint texture, and confirming the hat's radius and position properly cover the head without gaps at the back. Attaching goggles to the hat bone, then working out the hair spike geometry so the base radius and position poke out just below the hat's edge without clipping through it.

I'm figuring out the spike dimensions—base radius 0.1 at y 1.045, tapering to a tip radius 0.175 at y 1.0 with slight jitter, spaced across 13 spikes around the front arc. Then I'm placing the ears outward and tilted up, positioning the nose as a small sphere, and calculating the eye placement using a normalized direction vector to set the correct distance from center.

Now I'm computing exact eye and pupil positions along that vector, sizing the eye whites and pupils so they protrude slightly from the head surface, and adding a small highlight sphere offset above each pupil. I'm placing the eyebrows just above the eyes, checking their y-coordinates against the head's surface curvature to make sure they sit correctly on top.

Computing the normalized y-offset confirms it works out fine. I'm now working out nose and moustache placement using the same helper function, computing surface normals and offsetting by small radii to position them correctly below the nose.

Still computing placement coordinates...

I'm placing the cheek as a pink sphere, then working through jaw geometry — a scaled sphere for the lower skin, a mouth box carved inside, and beard patches as spheres positioned along the sides of the head using the same bone-relative coordinate system.

For the beard itself, I'm lofting a tube shape down through a series of stations along the jaw and chin, each with its own width and height, blended through a smooth curve so the cross-section tapers naturally from the jaw down to a point, with the tube's local axes aligned to the front-back and side directions of the face.

I'm placing six beard locks or spikes near the bottom with tips pointing down and outward, colored with a lighter beard tone, plus a small mustache bridge piece above. For the skeleton, I'm naming the joint "neck" as a single parent joint, adding a short cylinder for the visible neck skin, and now I'm starting work on the treasure pack geometry, including a tiny hinge cylinder for the lid at the back.

Writing part helper function...

Writing import statements...

I'm reconsidering the stripes texture — deciding to drop it since it risks looking too noisy on the sleeves, sticking with mottle instead for a subtler effect.

Now I'm building the clock face geometry, computing polar coordinates for the 12 tick marks around the dial with thicker lines at the 12/3/6/9 positions.

Checking the SVG orientation, then adding hands that run from center outward to specific angle positions, plus gauge arcs drawn clockwise from the top for the dial indicators.

Now I'm working out the spiral and coil geometry, passing center and starting points as arrays with radius and turn parameters, then building a catmull-rom arch from the coil's endpoint.

Still writing geometry...

I'm working out the pouch's radial embedding and positioning the wrench so it sits mostly hidden inside the pouch body, with only part of it protruding above the top edge near the belt line.

Now I'm placing the screwdriver similarly, keeping the shaft hidden inside the pouch while letting the wooden handle stick out above, roughly parallel to the wrench.

For the tool loadout, I'm deciding the right pouch holds a wrench plus a driver, while the left pouch gets two differently-colored screwdrivers for variety, skipping any extra tunic details for now and making sure the jaw role and rod helper are set up correctly before writing out the full tool placement code.

Now I'm setting up the bandolier as a draped path with a box-section sweep rigged to the chest bone so it stays rigid rather than deforming with nearby joints, confirming the sweep function signature works with a radius callback in that form.

For the vials, I'm placing five along the band at even intervals, alternating glass, amber, and purple colors with a glow strength and small brass cap cylinders on top, noting the beard will cover the center ones while the ends stay visible. Now I'm finalizing the file and checking which parts need the glow effect applied, like the lens and lantern glass.

I'm deciding on a single puff sphere near the hat's bell tip at a height that keeps the overall bounding box reasonable, skipping a second puff to avoid overcomplicating the silhouette. Writing leg point arrays and chain definitions...

Adding foot and toe joints...
